## The Temporal Architecture of the DPRH Sequence

In the DPRH model, each phase follows an overlapping but broadly sequential temporal order. Yet across different treatment modalities, these phases unfold on markedly different timescales. The most conspicuous distinction among plasticity-enhancing treatments may not be their molecular targets but their temporal dynamics: how rapidly they produce clinical effects, how long those effects persist, and what inter-session intervals are required for optimal outcomes. Understanding these temporal differences is essential for designing rational combination strategies.

## ECT

ECT delivers its disruption in seconds. The generalized seizure produces massive depolarization, glutamate release, and subsequent synaptic depression. Following this, postictal suppression blankets cortical networks within minutes [@AZUMA2007]. The slower emergence of postictal delta and theta slowing may persist for hours to days.

The plasticity window following an ECT session spans approximately 24–72 hours. Molecular markers defining this window include BDNF elevation (peak at 12–24 hours, sustained 48–72 hours), NMDA receptor subunit ratio shifts (12–48 hours), enhanced LTP inducibility in hippocampal slices (persisting 3–5 days), and immediate early gene protein products (sustained hours to days).

Standard ECT scheduling creates overlapping plasticity windows, with each session's window (3–7 days) extending into the subsequent treatment. This results in cumulative BDNF increases, sustained elevation of plasticity-related transcription, and progressive hippocampal volume increases. To prevent these windows from closing before the next session, a minimum of three sessions per week appears necessary [@Husain2004]. Conversely, spacing closer than 48 hours may cause excessive glutamate release and seizure threshold changes without enhanced efficacy.

In clinical terms, initial response emerges rapidly: the CORE study reported that about half of the patients showed early response after only three sessions [@Husain2004]. The entire course usually lasts 2–4 weeks across 6–12 sessions. However, without maintenance treatment, the six-month relapse rate reaches 84% [@sackeimEtAl2001].

## Ketamine/Esketamine

Ketamine's action is extremely rapid. A single intravenous infusion produces symptom reduction within hours, with some patients reporting improvement during the infusion itself [@Zarate2006]. This rapidity is attributed to its blockade of NMDA receptors, which triggers a compensatory glutamate surge that activates AMPA receptors. Also, it can directly activate mTOR bypassing the need for gradual TrkB-mediated pathway [@harraz2016]. The release of BDNF and mTOR-dependent synaptogenesis takes place within hours rather than the weeks required for monoaminergic agents.

However, the therapeutic effect of a single dose dissipates within 3–7 days, with relapse occurring at a median of 18–19 days after the last of a standard six-dose course [@Murrough2013; @Salloum2020]. This rapid decay reflects the transient nature of ketamine-induced synaptic remodeling. The initial burst of synaptic growth appears insufficient to establish durable circuit reorganization.

This rapid decay is mitigated by combination with antidepressants. In the relapse prevention trial by Daly et al.[@Daly2019], patients who achieved remission on esketamine plus oral antidepressant showed a median time to relapse of 635 days. This result underscores the critical role of pharmacological maintenance therapy.

## Psilocybin-Assisted Therapy

Psilocybin's acute pharmacological effect is time-limited: subjective effects begin within 20–40 minutes, peak at 90 minutes to 3 hours, and resolve within 4–6 hours. However, the therapeutic consequences are remarkably prolonged, extending months to over a year from a single or double administration [@Davis2021; @Gukasyan2022].

This combination of rapid onset and prolonged durability places psilocybin in a unique position among existing treatments. It should be noted, however, that psilocybin is rarely administered as a standalone pharmacological intervention; nearly all clinical protocols embed the drug experience within a structured psychotherapy framework. The integration psychotherapy surrounding each session may provide the directed environmental input required to guide adaptive rewiring [@Moliner2023]. Nevertheless, few other treatments are known to sustain a critical period of heightened plasticity for such an extended duration, suggesting that psilocybin's unique biological mechanism warrants further investigation.

## rTMS

Unlike ECT or psychedelics, standard rTMS operates through a different temporal logic. Individual sessions produce modest cortical excitability changes that are insufficient for clinical improvement. Meaningful therapeutic response requires the accumulation of many sessions, with most protocols delivering 20–30 sessions over 4–6 weeks. Even minimal effects take as long as 2 weeks to emerge [@OReardon2007].

This temporal profile reflects rTMS's mechanism as a targeted, circuit-level intervention. Rather than the global disruption of ECT or the widespread serotonergic perturbation of psychedelics, rTMS operates primarily as a local circuit rewiring process. The extended treatment course may be understood as a slow and deliberate sculpting of the neural landscape. Accordingly, relapse rates following rTMS monotherapy are comparatively lower than those observed after ECT or ketamine. Naturalistic follow-up studies report response maintenance rates of approximately 66.5% at 3 months, 52.9% at 6 months, and 46.3% at 12 months [@Carpenter2012].

The SAINT/SNT (Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy) protocol has achieved a degree of success in combining the advantages of both rTMS and ECT by delivering intensive, repeated stimulation within a compressed timeframe. Typically delivering 10 sessions per day over just 5 days, this accelerated protocol achieves remission rates of 79% in a double-blind RCT [@Cole2022], rivaling ECT in both speed and efficacy. Follow-up data show that over 70% of responders maintain gains at one month, with approximately 40% sustaining remission at three months [@Cole2020].

## SSRIs

As is well established, SSRIs require 3–6 weeks to achieve clinically meaningful effects. This protracted timeline reflects the multi-stage sequence underlying SSRI efficacy. The first days produce serotonin transporter occupancy and autoreceptor activation (disruption phase). Over the subsequent weeks, autoreceptor desensitization permits genuine enhancement of serotonergic tone, BDNF expression increases, and neurogenesis is initiated (potentiation phase). This potentiation phase, maturing at weeks 2–6, creates the conditions for DMN normalization, corticolimbic reconnection, and dendritic spine remodeling (rewiring phase) that emerge at weeks 4–12 of treatment.

Among the modalities discussed, SSRIs uniquely engage all four phases of the DPRH sequence. While their disruption is gentle and their potentiation slow to mature, the sustained neuromodulation acts as a constant impetus for stable rewiring. This may explain why SSRIs have been used as adjuncts to other treatment modalities: they supply the stabilization component that ECT, ketamine, and psilocybin inherently lack.

## Comparative Temporal Framework

The following table summarizes the temporal profiles across modalities:

| Modality | Onset of Action | Acute Treatment Duration | Inter-Session Interval | Remission Rate | Durability (Without Maintenance) | Maintenance Requirement |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| **Ketamine IV** | 2–4 hours | 2 weeks (6 infusions) | 2–3 days | \~50–60% | Median 18–19 days to relapse | Repeated infusions or oral antidepressant required |
| **ECT** | \~1 week (3 sessions) | 2–4 weeks (6–12 sessions) | 2–3 days | \~75% | 84% relapse at 6 months | Maintenance ECT or pharmacotherapy required |
| **Psilocybin** | Within 1 day | 1–2 sessions (1–3 weeks apart) | 1–3 weeks | \~29–54% | Months to 12+ months | Under investigation (comparatively durable) |
| **Standard rTMS** | 2–4 weeks | 4–6 weeks (20–30 sessions) | Daily (weekdays) | \~20–30% | \~46% response at 12 months | Maintenance rTMS may be needed |
| **SAINT/SNT** | 5 days | 5 days (50 sessions) | 50 minutes (within day) | \~79–90% | 70%+ at 1 month, \~40% at 3 months | Limited long-term data |
| **SSRIs** | 2–4 weeks | 6–8 weeks (assessment) | Continuous daily dosing | \~30–40% | High relapse upon discontinuation | 6 months to indefinite |
